items.content:
[This article was first published on R on Zhenguo Zhang's Blog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.
Zhenguo Zhang’s Blog https://fortune9.netlify.app/2026/10/16/statistics-collinearity-in-regression/ – 
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(broom)

Problem

When performing regression analysis, you may encounter two or more predictors that are highly correlated. This is called collinearity or multicollinearity. It can cause problems in estimating the regression coefficients and interpreting the results.

In this post, I will show how collinearity can affect regression analysis, how to detect collinearity, and how to deal with it.

Example: one predictor is a linear function of another predictor

Let’s simulate data with the following variables:

  • X1: a random variable drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
  • X2: another random variable drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, independent of X1.
  • Z: a variable linearly related to X2, defined as Z = 5*X2 + noise, where the noise is drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
  • Y: a linear combination of X1 and X2 plus noise, defined as Y = 3*X1 + 2*X2 + noise, where the noise is drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
set.seed(123)
n <- 100
X1 <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
X2 <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
Z <- 5 * X2 + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
Y <- 3 * X1 + 2 * X2 + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

The correlation coefficients among the three predictors are:

kable(cor(cbind(X1, X2, Z)), caption="Correlation of the predictors")
Table 1: Correlation of the predictors
X1 X2 Z
X1 1.0000000 -0.0495321 -0.0730836
X2 -0.0495321 1.0000000 0.9814767
Z -0.0730836 0.9814767 1.0000000

Now let’s fit two linear regression models: one with X1 and X2 as predictors, and another with X1, X2, and Z as predictors. We will then examine how the following metrics change: coefficients, standard errors, t-values, p-values, R-squared, adjusted R-squared.

fit1 <- lm(Y ~ X1 + X2)
fit2 <- lm(Y ~ X1 + X2 + Z)
coef_results <- rbind(
  tidy(fit1) %>% mutate(model = "fit1"),
  tidy(fit2) %>% mutate(model = "fit2")
)
# move model to the first column
coef_results <- coef_results %>% select(model, everything())
# now R-squared and adjusted R-squared
rsq_results <- rbind(
  glance(fit1) %>% mutate(model = "fit1"),
  glance(fit2) %>% mutate(model = "fit2")
) %>%
  select(model, everything())
kable(coef_results, caption = "The coefficients and statistics")
Table 2: The coefficients and statistics
model term estimate std.error statistic p.value
fit1 (Intercept) -0.0270771 0.1058626 -0.2557758 0.7986656
fit1 X1 2.9521917 0.1154749 25.5656651 0.0000000
fit1 X2 2.0448517 0.1090059 18.7590842 0.0000000
fit2 (Intercept) -0.0193261 0.1073437 -0.1800395 0.8575011
fit2 X1 2.9445494 0.1168766 25.1936688 0.0000000
fit2 X2 2.3331532 0.5743463 4.0622761 0.0000993
fit2 Z -0.0573870 0.1122308 -0.5113302 0.6102939 
kable(rsq_results, caption = "The goodness of fit")
Table 2: The goodness of fit
model r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value df logLik AIC BIC deviance df.residual nobs
fit1 0.9082614 0.9063699 1.047502 480.1763 0 2 -145.0117 298.0234 308.4441 106.4342 97 100
fit2 0.9085106 0.9056516 1.051513 317.7673 0 3 -144.8757 299.7514 312.7773 106.1452 96 100

As the results show, the first model, fit1, roughly captures the true relationship in the simulated data, and both coefficients are highly statistically significant.

Adding Z to the regression model produces several changes: (1) the coefficient for X2 becomes smaller, (2) its standard error increases more than fivefold, and (3) the p-value for the coefficient test consequently increases substantially. Overall, the model’s R-squared changes little, but its AIC and BIC values increase, suggesting that the model with three predictors is less favorable than the model with two predictors.

In summary, including a predictor that is highly correlated with an existing predictor reduces the statistical significance of the existing predictor.

Example: two predictors with different levels of correlation

Now let’s simulate datasets containing two variables with different levels of correlation. We will use Cholesky decomposition to simulate the data.

First, let’s write a function that simulates data for a specified correlation coefficient:

simulate_correlated_data<-function(rho, n=100, seed=NULL) {
  if(is.null(seed)) {
    seed < Sys.time()
  }
  set.seed(seed)
  x <- rnorm(n)
  z <- rnorm(n)
  y <- rho*x + sqrt(1-rho^2)*z
  return(cbind(x,y))
}

Now let’s simulate five datasets with target correlations of 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, and 0.95 between the two predictors. We will also make both predictors contribute to the response variable so that we can examine how different levels of correlation affect the regression fit:

n<-100
rhos<-c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 0.95)
simulated_data <- lapply(rhos, simulate_correlated_data, n=n)
# let's calculate the correlation coefficients for the simulated data
simulated_rhos<-sapply(simulated_data, function(d) cor(d[,"x"],d[, "y"]))
kable(cbind(expected_rho=rhos, actual_rho=simulated_rhos))
expected_rho actual_rho
0.10 -0.0271945
0.30 0.3337500
0.50 0.5365344
0.80 0.8167663
0.95 0.9624687

The correlation coefficient, rho, in each simulated dataset may not exactly match the specified value because of random sampling, but we can still examine how the level of correlation affects the regression.

 fits <- lapply(simulated_data, function(d) {
          x1<-d[,"x"]
          x2<-d[, "y"]
          y <- 10*x1 + 3*x2 + rnorm(n)
          fit<-lm(y~x1 + x2)
          return(fit)
          } 
          )
coef_results<-lapply(seq_along(rhos),
                     function(i) {
                       tidy(fits[[i]]) %>%
                         mutate(rho = rhos[i]) %>%
                         select(rho, everything())
                     }
                     )
coef_results <- do.call(rbind, coef_results)
kable(coef_results, caption = "Regression statistics with different correlation strengths among predictors")
Table 3: Regression statistics with different correlation strengths among predictors
rho term estimate std.error statistic p.value
0.10 (Intercept) 0.1545731 0.1093261 1.4138713 0.1606012
0.10 x1 10.0038407 0.1047198 95.5296414 0.0000000
0.10 x2 3.0724520 0.1118900 27.4595781 0.0000000
0.30 (Intercept) 0.0349345 0.1183168 0.2952627 0.7684243
0.30 x1 9.8936718 0.1339565 73.8573235 0.0000000
0.30 x2 3.0068927 0.1113956 26.9929282 0.0000000
0.50 (Intercept) 0.1417142 0.0972655 1.4569831 0.1483507
0.50 x1 10.0727790 0.1156101 87.1271918 0.0000000
0.50 x2 2.9767374 0.1173528 25.3657122 0.0000000
0.80 (Intercept) -0.0609381 0.0979742 -0.6219812 0.5354135
0.80 x1 10.3154854 0.1709446 60.3440164 0.0000000
0.80 x2 2.7154226 0.1638409 16.5735364 0.0000000
0.95 (Intercept) -0.1158642 0.0971670 -1.1924234 0.2360041
0.95 x1 10.0497393 0.3537788 28.4068467 0.0000000
0.95 x2 2.9023068 0.3443712 8.4278435 0.0000000

Let’s plot all the metrics:

coef_results <- coef_results %>% 
    mutate(rho = factor(rho)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = estimate:p.value,
      names_to = "metric",
      values_to = "value"
    )
plt <- ggplot(coef_results, aes(x=rho, y=value)) +
      geom_point(aes(color=term)) +
      facet_wrap(~ metric, ncol=2, scales="free_y") +
      theme(legend.position = "top")
plt

The plots show the following patterns as the correlation between the predictors increases:

  • The estimated coefficients change little, although some variation remains.
  • The p-values for both predictors remain very small.
  • The test statistics become smaller as rho increases.
  • The standard errors increase as rho increases.
  • Based on the last two observations, the p-values for the predictors should become larger, i.e., less significant.

In summary, when the predictors in a regression are correlated, the test for each coefficient becomes less statistically significant, even though the magnitudes of the coefficients remain close to the values used to simulate the data.

Takeaways

  • When one predictor, Z, is a linear function of another predictor, X, and has no direct relationship with the response variable, including Z makes the test for the true predictor X less statistically significant. The coefficient for Z may not be significant because, after accounting for X, Z has no effect on Y.
  • When two predictors both affect Y, the statistical significance of their coefficients decreases as the correlation between the predictors increases, even though the magnitudes of the coefficients may remain close to the true values.

Taken together, these examples suggest that you may want to exclude certain variables from your regression unless you know they affect the response or want to examine the effects of other predictors after controlling for those variables.

items.content:
[This article was first published on The Jumping Rivers Blog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

If you plan to learn R or Python in the new year, book before the end of November. Our spring 2027 data science training courses run from January to June, and early bird pricing on the first one ends on 29 November.

There are 22 courses on the schedule. All of them run live online, and the trainers are data scientists and engineers who spend the rest of their week on client projects. Each course runs over two afternoons, 13:30 to 17:00 UK time. The Bayesian inference course is the exception: it runs over four.

Three routes through our spring 2027 training courses

The courses are scheduled so you can take them in order. There are three obvious routes, each ending with a set of skills you can use at work the following week.

Learning R from scratch

Start with Introduction to R on 11–12 January. Data Wrangling in the Tidyverse follows on 25–26 January, then Data Visualisation with ggplot2 on 1–2 February and Programming with R on 8–9 February. That gets you from your first script to writing your own functions in a month.

Why take this route: Clean, chart and automate your data in code. Monthly reporting becomes a script you rerun in minutes, with fewer manual errors.

January too soon? The same four courses run again between 12 April and 11 May. If you are still deciding whether R is worth the time, we wrote about why learning R is a good career move.

Learning Python

Introduction to Python runs on 15–16 February. Programming with Python follows on 22–23 February, and Data Visualisation with Python on 1–2 March. The same three run again in May and June.

Why take this route: Analyse data in pandas, automate repeat tasks and produce report-ready charts, in the same language as your engineering team. It is also the groundwork for machine learning in Python.

Statistics and machine learning in R

This route is for people who already use R. Statistical Modelling with R on 8–9 March covers hypothesis testing, regression, clustering and principal components analysis. Machine Learning with Tidymodels on 15–16 March and Advanced Machine Learning with Tidymodels on 22–23 March take you through pre-processing, model fitting and tuning.

Why take this route: Build, validate and tune predictive models in tidymodels, and explain which variables drive them. Your team moves from reporting what happened to forecasting what happens next, with evidence for how far to trust it.

Two courses that run once this spring

Introduction to Bayesian Inference using RStan runs over four afternoons, 18–21 January. You write Stan programs for a range of statistical models and learn to read the MCMC diagnostics in R. It is the only date for it in the first half of 2027.

Reporting with Quarto runs on 21–22 June. You build reports, slides and documents straight from R or Python code, so the numbers in the report change when the data does. It pairs well with the ideas in our post on reproducible analytical pipelines.

Whether you want to start from scratch, or improve your skills, Jumping Rivers has a training course for you.

Early bird deadlines

Early bird pricing ends about six weeks before each course. Booking closes a week before the start date. The first three deadlines are:

  • 29 November for Introduction to R
  • 6 December for Bayesian inference
  • 13 December for Data Wrangling in the Tidyverse

Dates for the second half of 2027 will follow.

Using this year’s training budget

If your team has training budget left this December, booking a January course now spends it before the year ends. It also gets you the early bird price, because every January deadline falls before Christmas.

What you get on every course

  • PDF notes and scripts to keep
  • Live demonstrations and hands-on exercises
  • Time with the trainer to ask questions about your own work

We have run more than 1,000 courses, for organisations including NHS Scotland, Shell, Wessex Water and the Royal Statistical Society.

Training a whole team

Every course in our full catalogue can also run privately for one team, using your data and your tools. Group bookings and returning clients get a discount. Email training@jumpingrivers.com with the size of the team and what they need to learn.

See the full public schedule and book a place.
